scope: Fort Victoria as it stood in September 1860, with the two log bastions, cedar palisade, Fort Street gates, bell tower, and researched exterior courtyard buildings and paths.
geometryBasis: The historical east gate follows Fort Street on Government Street, and the west gate follows the same line toward Wharf Street. City survey and commemorative brickwork tie the northern palisade and northeast bastion to Government and Bastion Square. The southwest bastion is inside the present Broughton and Wharf corner. Fawcett’s eyewitness text and the Maritime Museum tour support reconstruction of a nearly rectangular enclosure inside the four modern streets. The width is an estimate from the street and marker alignment, with the north–south extent close to the roughly 465 feet described after the 1847 enlargement.
sectionBasis: The exact September 1860 Crease watercolor and contemporary published copy establish the southwest octagonal bastion and stockade. Five original illustrations published in Fawcett’s 1912 eyewitness memoir show the same bastion, different north and east views, both the whitewashed hipped buildings and the bell tower and gate facing Fort Street. Fawcett places offices and residences east, stores north, barns south and the bell tower in the yard. Earlier reports and construction notes provide typical scales and materials.

primaryWrittenSources.notes: Parks Canada identifies the former downtown fort site and two bastions and palisade.

Vavasour's written 1845 survey notes describe octagonal bastions with 5-foot lower sides, squared pine structures, armament, and cedar pickets reported at 20 feet. The UVic plan reproduction is explicitly restricted. Use the transcribed observations and seek unrestricted original prints for any graphical controls.
Edgar Fawcett's 1912 eyewitness memoir has original published photographs captioned Fort Victoria, 1859 and Bastion at S.W. corner of Fort, and discussion of the altered enclosure.
Toronto Public Library marks its H.O. Tiedemann panorama public domain. Printed and published in London on 13 June 1860. The legend identifies the fort for the view across the harbor.

Museum researcher dates the historical six-part fort panorama and written notice of December 14, 1860 dismantling. The 1860 pictures appear in early Maynard albums. Use publication proof for each exact photo before inclusion.
Municipal report establishes the commemorative brick trace along Government Street, the northeast bastion marker and the continuation through Bastion Square.
Maritime Museum walking tour identifies the southwest bastion position inside the present city block, the outlines of the northeastern bastion and the documented inner yard well and bell tower.
Transcriptions of company correspondence describe 18-foot early palisades, 60 by 30 foot stores and houses, 60 by 40 foot officers’ house and the 1847 enlargement and rebuilt southwest bastion.
